content: The methodologists were tasked with retrieving, synthesizing, and evaluating evidence. This process was preceded by the formulation of key questions and the selection of outcomes in collaboration with the Guideline Development Group and a WHO Steering Group. They conducted a systematic review of the literature and assessed the quality and certainty of the evidence using the GRADE approach. Decision tables were prepared to guide the Guideline Development Group in formulating recommendations during a face-to-face meeting in Geneva in January 2015. This meeting was co-chaired by an independent methodologist familiar with WHO’s procedures and standards for guideline development and a member of the Guideline Development Group. The draft guidelines underwent external peer review by five experts with diverse expertise in onchocerciasis, lymphatic filariasis, and malaria. Their comments were used to refine the final document. Two key questions were formulated: (1) Which diagnostic tests or combinations of tests can validly and reliably demonstrate the interruption of O. volvulus transmission for stopping mass drug administration (MDA)? (2) Which diagnostic tests or combinations of tests can validly and reliably confirm the interruption of O. volvulus transmission at the end of post-treatment surveillance? The systematic review addressed these two key questions. Eligible populations included human populations at risk for onchocerciasis and black flies (Simulium species) in endemic regions, as they are the vectors of O. volvulus. Studies included those that implemented diagnostic tests for measuring the elimination of O. volvulus, either individually or in combinations. Evidence from studies with validated reference standards or comparisons of test versions was also included. The primary outcome was the absence of infection recrudescence, meaning a negative test at the time of Key Question 1 predicted a negative test at the time of Key Question 2. The first question determined the interruption of transmission and the end of MDA, while the second confirmed the end of post-treatment surveillance. The experts used the GRADE approach to assess the quality of evidence and formulate recommendations. Each recommendation was accompanied by an assessment of the certainty of the evidence, categorized as high, moderate, low, or very low. The Guideline Development Group reviewed the key questions and formulated recommendations based on the evidence. Discussions were structured around decision tables that included criteria such as diagnostic test accuracy, evidence certainty, resource requirements, cost, equity, feasibility, and acceptability. Recommendations were adopted by consensus or, if necessary, by a two-thirds majority vote. Strong recommendations were made when the desirable effects of adherence clearly outweighed the undesirable effects, while conditional recommendations were made when the balance of effects was less certain. The draft guidelines were externally reviewed before finalization, with clarifications added as needed. All members of the Guideline Development Group and methodologists signed WHO Declaration of Interest forms. Two members reported receiving research grants or consulting fees, but these were deemed not to constitute significant conflicts of interest. The methodologists, who were not voting members or onchocerciasis experts, ensured objective evidence evaluation and accurate reflection of the evidence in the recommendations. There was limited direct comparative evidence on the use of different tests for verifying the elimination of human onchocerciasis. The best available evidence came from two prospective observational studies on transmission interruption leading to treatment cessation. Diagnostic test accuracy studies were generally conducted in high-prevalence populations, which do not reflect low-prevalence settings near transmission interruption. The standard reference test, skin snip microscopy, performs poorly in low-prevalence settings. For demonstrating transmission interruption or elimination, the quality of evidence for entomological assessment using O-150 PCR (Poolscreen) in black flies was rated high, while evidence for epidemiological assessments such as Ov-16 serology, skin snip microscopy, and ocular morbidity was rated low. O-150 PCR testing in black flies is recommended to demonstrate the interruption of O. volvulus transmission in human populations receiving MDA. This test is highly specific and cost-effective, especially when larger pools of flies are used. However, implementation feasibility depends on factors such as procurement policies, Ministry of Health support, frontline health facility involvement, and health worker attitudes. Community engagement is crucial for test acceptability and intervention success. Ov-16 serology testing in children under 10 years of age is recommended to demonstrate the interruption of O. volvulus transmission in human populations receiving MDA. This test is minimally invasive and more acceptable than skin snipping. However, challenges include the need for two days to test an average sample. The test is cost-effective compared to continuing MDA and can be implemented with strong community participation and support from non-governmental organizations. The desirable consequences of using Ov-16 serology testing outweigh the undesirable consequences in most settings. The existence of regional laboratories serving large administrative areas is essential for implementing these tests. Sampling should follow standardized procedures, and laboratory quality control must be regularly monitored. Testing should be conducted annually until the end of post-treatment surveillance. Further research is needed to define standardized protocols for fly catching and to improve diagnostic test accuracy in low-prevalence settings.
